transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Noah Green (Redwood Solutions); Maya Chen (Harborline Head of Platform), Diego Alvarez (Lead ML Eng), Priya Rao (Security), Tom Bishop (SRE)

Summary:
Quick intro and goals: scope a 4-week POC to validate OpenAI-style API compatibility, streaming & function-calling behavior, structured JSON outputs, and run throughput/latency benchmarks against Harborline's freight assistant workload. Discussed success criteria (latency/quality/throughput), workload sizing, hosting mode options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), security considerations (KMS, SSO, audit logs), and an initial timeline.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and acceptance metrics
- Workload characteristics and required sizing
- Benchmark plan and scripts
- SDK and endpoint mapping (OpenAI-style compatibility)
- Function/tool-calling and structured output schemas
- Security/compliance (KMS, SAML/SSO, data residency)
- Pilot timeline and responsibilities

Action items (recap included above)

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro from our side, im Samir, I'm the AE, with Lena who's our solutions engineer, and Noah who helps with the bench scripts.
[00:00:12] Maya: Hi, Maya here. thanks for joining. we've been evaluating a couple of different routes and want to run a short pilot to answer questions about latency and whether we can keep call volumes in-house.
[00:00:25] Samir: Great. can you outline the primary success criteria? that's the best place to start.
[00:00:31] Diego: Sure. For us: 1) Quality parity with current cloud provider outputs — must match current intent detection/categorization accuracy within 3% on our eval set. 2) Latency: p50 under 150ms for short queries (<256 tokens), p95 under 600ms, and 3) Throughput: sustain 30 concurrent active sessions — typical request size ~700 tokens, peak ingestion 75 qps across the fleet.
[00:01:05] Lena: okay, that helps. couple clarifications — when you say 700 tokens that's per request or including context?
[00:01:10] Diego: average request includes a 200 token user message plus up to 500 token system/prefix/history so yes ~700 tokens total per call.
[00:01:20] Tom: and we have the usual bursts, shipping window spikes where concurrency jumps 3x for about 5-10 minutes.
[00:01:27] Samir: noted. timing and burst behavior are important for the autoscaling and batching profile. we generally recommend two parallel experiments in the POC: 1) hosted Redwood API to validate API-compat and quality quickly, 2) a dedicated pilot (reserved GPUs) to validate sustained throughput and tail latency.
[00:01:43] Priya: security side — we need to confirm data residency (EU-only for some customers), KMS controls for encryption-at-rest, and audit logs with per-request metadata. do you support customer-managed keys?
[00:01:55] Lena: yes we support KMS integrations and HSM-backed key control on Private deployments; hosted can be configured for customer KMS with a limited set of providers. we'll send the whitepaper. audit logs and per-token billing traces are available in the Redwood Console.
[00:02:10] Maya: timeline wise we're aiming to decide on a vendor by the end of November so a 4-week pilot starting early November would fit.
[00:02:18] Samir: that's doable. proposed POC schedule: week 0 — onboarding + SDK integration + data and traces; week 1 — small-scale throughput/latency bench and function-calling validation; week 2 — full-scale benchmark, stress tests and quality evals; week 3 — analyze results, tweak quant/ batching, handoff decision.
[00:02:34] Diego: what does SDK integration look like? we have an existing client that talks to OpenAI endpoints and uses function-calling heavily — can we point it at Redwood with minimal changes?
[00:02:44] Lena: yes, we provide OpenAI-style endpoints that map the same request/response semantics. we also have a drop-in SDK with the same method names and streaming semantics. you should be able to switch base URL and API key and have most flows work. caveats: model_name mapping (we have different model ids), and some advanced headers for routing/quantization.
[00:03:02] Noah: we'll share an SDK sample repo with a tiny adapter. we'll also include examples for structured-output enforcement (JSON schema) and function-calling with retries/parsing heuristics.
[00:03:13] Diego: for function-calling we rely on deterministic JSON outputs, otherwise our downstream parsers blow up. how do you handle structured output reliability?
[00:03:21] Lena: couple strategies: 1) structured output via explicit JSON schema + validation step, 2) post-checks with regeneration on mismatch, 3) a function-calling hook that returns typed payloads. we'll show a pattern where the model is prompted with a strict schema and we run a lightweight validator server-side. also prefix caching (KV cache) reduces context recompute for repeated prompts.
[00:03:43] Tom: any concerns about streaming chunks breaking JSON? we stream token-by-token to the client.
[00:03:49] Lena: streaming is supported. pattern we recommend is to stream text and finalize with a compact JSON chunk; we also offer structured streaming where we emit JSON events. there are tradeoffs but we'll include both examples.
[00:04:03] Maya: benchmarks — what metrics will you capture?
[00:04:07] Noah: we'll capture p50/p90/p95 token latency, end-to-end request times, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost-per-token. for the pilot we'll run scenario sets: short chat, long context (2k tokens), and tool-calling (function-calling included).
[00:04:23] Diego: for cost considerations, do you have estimates for quantized models vs fp16 on A100s?
[00:04:29] Samir: initial roughs: a quantized variant can reduce GPU memory and cost materially but may add some latency variability. we'll include both model families in the benchmark: a high-performance fp16 model for latency-focused tests and a 4-bit quantized model for cost-focused runs.
[00:04:43] Priya: we also need to know about auditability — can we get a per-request signed audit record and retention controls?
[00:04:49] Lena: yes, audit logs with per-request metadata and optional signed attestations are available on Dedicated and Private. hosted can retain logs and export to your SIEM; retention windows configurable as part of the enterprise add-on.
[00:05:01] Maya: what about SSO and RBAC? our org uses SAML and fine-grained role separation — devs vs production operators.
[00:05:07] Lena: we support SAML SSO and OIDC; RBAC supports role scoping for models, routes and billing tokens. we'll attach the SSO integration guide.
[00:05:16] Diego: back to benchmarks: we want to reproduce a peak shipping window — 75 qps with bursts to 220 qps for 5-10 minutes — and see p95 under 600ms. is that realistic?
[00:05:26] Samir: for the hosted tier we can often hit that at smaller sequence lengths with autoscaling; sustained peaks it's better to test on Dedicated. The POC will run both: hosted to validate integration and quality, dedicated to validate tail latency and cost for sustained load.
[00:05:40] Tom: what's the expected infra footprint for the dedicated pilot to mimic our peak?
[00:05:45] Lena: based on your numbers (700 tokens avg, 75 sustained qps) we estimate needing approximately 4 x H100-class GPU instances for the throughput/latency targets with room for bursting. quantization and batching policies could reduce that to 2-3 nodes in some cases. the bench will validate exact sizing.
[00:06:03] Diego: and can the runtime route lower-priority traffic to cheaper models during overloads?
[00:06:07] Samir: yes, smart routing and fallback policies are part of the platform — you can configure a tiered policy that routes to smaller, cheaper model variants during capacity pressure and failover to a CPU-based fallback if needed.
[00:06:17] Maya: acceptance criteria — besides latency/throughput/quality, we need a clear operational checklist: SSO + RBAC working, KMS + audit logs validated, and integration with our monitoring. can you provide the checklist?
[00:06:29] Samir: we'll provide a POC acceptance checklist that includes those items plus sample queries and a quality gate.
[00:06:34] Priya: one more compliance question: do you do annual SOC2? and is the private deployment air-gapped possible?
[00:06:40] Lena: we have SOC2 Type II; Private on-prem packaging is possible for air-gapped setups, though that's typically a longer procurement path. we'll include the compliance pack.
[00:06:51] Diego: what does end-to-end latency look like when you enable function-calling + tool invocation? we have a function that hits an internal graph DB and returns small JSON — that roundtrip has to be under 400ms p95 to keep UX sane.
[00:07:03] Lena: function-calling introduces extra hops, we'll instrument the trace to show model inference time vs webhook latency. for POC we'll run a mock hook in your VPC to get realistic numbers.
[00:07:12] Samir: okay, let's define deliverables for the POC: 1) Redwood sends SOW + bench harness and sample SDK 2) Harborline provides traces + a small set of prompts/expected outputs 3) schedule bench run and a demo of structured-output reliability 4) security review completion.
[00:07:28] Maya: sounds good. who will own the bench scripts?
[00:07:32] Noah: Redwood owns initial harness and will hand over scripts; we'll expect Harborline to run them in private env if you want to test Private. we'll also run them from our hosted lab to reproduce results.
[00:07:43] Diego: small ask — include an OpenTelemetry trace schema so we can correlate request ids across our systems.
[00:07:48] Lena: we'll include OTEL spans and a sample Jaeger collector config.
[00:07:53] Tom: and for the SDK adapter, do you plan to support streaming chunk aggregation for our mobile clients?
[00:07:59] Noah: yes, we provide streaming SDK helpers that aggregate on the client side and optionally emit final structured events. will include sample code.
[00:08:09] [pause, background noise]
[00:08:25] Priya: quick question — if we need EU-residency only, can hosted provide region restriction?
[00:08:31] Lena: Hosted can pin to regions and we have EU-only hosting options; for strict commercials we recommend Private or Dedicated in a specific region.
[00:08:39] Maya: ok great. timeline recap?
[00:08:43] Samir: Kickoff (this week): exchange artifacts. Week of Nov 9: bench runs. Nov 16: analysis + optimization. By end of Nov: decision.
[00:08:54] Diego: can you also include a cost sensitivity matrix — cost per 1M tokens for fp16 vs quant?
[00:08:59] Samir: yes will include a sensitivity table showing cost ranges and expected latency tradeoffs.
[00:09:05] Maya: any blockers on our side? we need to confirm who'll run which bench steps and whether we want to test Private or not.
[00:09:12] Priya: security review timeline: we can turn around questionnaire answers in 48 hours.
[00:09:15] Samir: perfect. we'll target sending the SOW and bench harness by Thursday (2026-11-05).
[00:09:22] Noah: one small note on evals — please flag any prompt groups that hit PII or regulated content; we'll separate those into a compliance bench.
[00:09:30] Diego: yes will do.
[00:09:33] Maya: thanks all. next meeting after bench run to go over results?
[00:09:37] Samir: yep, we'll schedule the results review during the week of Nov 16.
[00:09:42] [wrap up small talk]
[00:10:10] END (notes: remaining ~50 minutes were Q&A and deeper clarifications, logs truncated)

Appendix - quick bench plan (summarized):
- Scenario A: short chat
  - avg tokens per request: 150
  - target sustained qps: 40
  - goals: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 400ms
- Scenario B: medium context (700 tokens)
  - target sustained qps: 25
  - goals: p50 < 200ms, p95 < 600ms
- Scenario C: long context (2k tokens)
  - target sustained qps: 8
  - goals: p50 < 400ms, p95 < 900ms
- Scenario D: function-calling (webhook + model inference)
  - synthetic webhook latency: 50-200ms
  - overall p95 goal: < 600ms

Bench metrics to capture: p50/p90/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU util, cost per 1M tokens (fp16 vs 4-bit), failure rates, retry counts, memory pressure, and OTA trace correlation ids.
